problem: Value Iteration Networks (VINs), the standard differentiable path-planning module used inside navigation agents (e.g. CMP, QMDP-Net), are hard to optimize. Training oscillates between epochs, final performance depends strongly on the random seed and on hyperparameters, VIN diverges or degrades with kernel sizes larger than 3–5, and it needs many recurrent iterations to propagate information over long paths.
motivation: Differentiable planners are a key building block of end-to-end navigation architectures, so their optimization failures limit the downstream agents. The driving observation is that the VIN update is simply an ungated convolutional RNN: its recurrent state has dimension one, it uses an unusual channel-wise max-pooling nonlinearity, and its kernels are 3×3. Such RNNs are known to suffer from vanishing and exploding gradients, which gated recurrent units were designed to fix.
key_idea: Reframe VIN as a recurrent-convolutional network and replace its max-pooling value-iteration update with a gated ConvLSTM update, giving the Gated Path Planning Network (GPPN), which drops VIN's hand-designed inductive bias.
insight: The VIN's value-iteration inductive bias is not what makes differentiable planning work, and in practice it mainly causes optimization trouble. With gating, the planner trains stably, and GPPN's advantage over VIN grows as data shrinks: at 10k samples NEWS %Opt is 97.8 vs 90.3, at 100k it is 99.9 vs 97.3 (Table 4). This contradicts the hypothesis that VIN's bias helps generalization. The ablations that show this: Table 1, where VIN drops from 93.9 to 86.8 %Opt on NEWS when F goes 5→9 while GPPN improves to 99.2 at F=11, so gating unlocks larger kernels and fewer iterations; Table 5, where seed std is ≤0.2 for GPPN vs up to 1.5 for VIN; and Table 6, where GPPN reaches 95% val %Opt in 5–6 epochs while VIN never reaches it on NEWS. The appendix Hyper-VIN shows that a VIN with per-cell weights predicted from the map still falls well short of exact value iteration even though VI is in its hypothesis class (NEWS 75.1 vs 94.2 %Opt), which again points to optimization as the bottleneck.
method: VIN as a conv-RNN: rewrites the VIN update V̄^(k) = max_ā(W^R_ā R̄_[F] + W^V_ā V̄^(k-1)_[F]) as an RNN step with a linear map over input and previous state followed by a channel-wise max nonlinearity. This exposes four quirks: hidden dimension 1, max-pool activation, sparse local weights, and kernel size 3.

GPPN gated update: replaces that step with an LSTM at every map cell. (h,c)^(k)_{i',j'} = LSTM(Σ_ā W^R_ā R̄_[i',j',F] + W^h_ā h^(k-1)_[i',j',F], c^(k-1)_{i',j'}), i.e. a weight-tied ConvLSTM unrolled K times over the maze plus goal map. It outputs a policy for every state.

Practical LSTM variant: the R̄ input is dropped after the first step, since the skip connection did not help. The F×F convolution over the previous hidden states produces a 1-channel map that is fed per position into a built-in LSTM, which amounts to a single shared input gate. Hidden size is 150 for GPPN vs 600 for VIN to roughly match parameter counts.

Large kernels and fewer iterations: kernel size F∈{3,5,7,9,11} and iteration count K∈{5,10,15,20,30} are swept, with K∈{14,28,56} for 28×28 mazes. Larger F grows the receptive field faster, so good policies need fewer iterations (K≤10).

3D ViZDoom map-inference front-end: first-person RGB screenshots from every cell and 4 orientations go through a CNN (32 8×8/s4 filters, then 64 4×4/s2 filters, then a 256-d linear layer). The 4 orientation features are concatenated into a 1024×m×m map. Two 3×3 conv layers (64 channels, then 1) predict the 1×m×m maze design, trained with an auxiliary BCE loss. The predicted design is stacked with the goal map and fed to VIN or GPPN.

Training and evaluation protocol: the policy is trained and evaluated directly on all states at once rather than on stochastically sampled rollouts, with early stopping on validation. Metrics are %Opt (share of states whose predicted path has optimal length) and %Suc (share of states whose predicted path reaches the goal).

setting.backbone: GPPN (ConvLSTM planner, hidden dim 150) trained from scratch; in 3D, plus a 2-conv-layer CNN image encoder and a map-prediction head
setting.training_data: Synthetic procedurally generated mazes: DFS recursive-backtracker trees with each wall deleted at probability d~U[0,1]. Default split is 25k/5k/5k train/val/test at 15×15; also 10k/2k/2k and 100k/10k/10k, and 25k at 28×28. The 3D ViZDoom set is 10k mazes with 4m² first-person RGB screenshots each. Training uses optimal-path supervision over all states, with no external data.
setting.observation: 2D: fully observed top-down binary maze map plus goal map (m×m; 4×m×m goal for Differential Drive). 3D: first-person RGB images taken at every position and all 4 orientations of the maze, plus goal map.
setting.action_space: Discrete grid moves: NEWS (4-connected), Moore (8-connected), or Differential Drive (forward / turn left or right 90°).
setting.simulator: Custom 2D grid-maze environment; ViZDoom (Doom engine) for 3D mazes
setting.privileged: The whole environment is given up front: the full top-down maze map (2D), or pre-captured first-person images from every cell and orientation (3D, equivalent to full pre-exploration). The goal location map is also provided. In 3D, the ground-truth maze design supervises an auxiliary loss during training.

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is used; all results are on the authors' own synthetic 2D grid mazes and ViZDoom 3D mazes, with held-out test splits of their own generated data. Test sets for N=10k/25k/100k differ in size (2k/5k/10k). Not extracted: the full (K,F) grid (Tables 1–3), seed variance on train/val (Table 5), epochs-to-threshold (Table 6), learning-rate sweep (Table 9), and Hyper-VIN vs VIN vs GPPN vs exact Value Iteration at half hidden size (Table 10; GPPN NEWS 98.9/99.3, DD 98.1/98.8). Hyperparameter sensitivity and learning curves appear only in figures (Figs. 2, 3, 5–7). Minor inconsistency: the text says 'GPPN 99.3 vs. VIN 98.3 for %Opt' for Diff. Drive 15×15, but Table 7 prints VIN 98.4.
results: On 15×15 2D mazes with 25k training samples, GPPN reaches 99.2 / 98.8 / 99.3 %Opt (NEWS / Moore / Diff. Drive) against VIN's 93.9 / 96.3 / 98.4. On 28×28 mazes it reaches 98.3 / 97.8 / 99.0 vs 93.0 / 95.0 / 93.8. GPPN also learns 2–5× faster, has far lower seed variance, and tolerates larger kernels. In 3D ViZDoom, where the map must be inferred from first-person RGB, GPPN beats VIN on NEWS (94.1 vs 79.0 test %Opt) and Moore (94.5 vs 84.6). It is worse on Diff. Drive (91.4 vs 96.9) because it overfits.
limitations: Evaluation is only on small, fully observed synthetic grid mazes (15×15, 28×28). There is no partial observability, no photorealistic or real-world navigation, and no integration into a downstream embodied agent.
The 3D setting assumes pre-captured first-person images at every cell and orientation, effectively full pre-exploration. GPPN overfits on Differential Drive there and underperforms VIN.

The paper offers no interpretability of what the gated planner computes; it drops VIN's value-iteration structure. GPPN also has about 4× the parameters per hidden unit, which the authors compensate for with a smaller hidden size.
compares_to: Hyper-VIN (own VIN variant with map-predicted untied weights)
